genZNote: Germ tube negative and increasingly fluconazole-resistant — exactly why a positive blood culture triggers susceptibility testing before anyone picks an antifungal.

morphology.shape: Small oval budding yeast cells; does not typically form pseudohyphae or true hyphae

habitat.naturalHabitat: Human gastrointestinal tract, oral cavity, and vagina as commensal flora
habitat.hostAssociation: Normal commensal in healthy individuals; increasingly important opportunistic pathogen in hospitalized/immunocompromised patients
habitat.reservoir: Human mucosal surfaces and GI tract

microscopy.stain: Gram stain or KOH wet mount
microscopy.appearance: Small oval budding yeast cells without pseudohyphae

culture.pigmentation: Pink to purple on CHROMagar Candida (distinguishes from green C. albicans)

identificationClues: Small budding yeast cells with no true hyphae or pseudohyphae — unlike C. albicans
Germ tube negative and chlamydospore negative
Pink to purple colonies on CHROMagar Candida (green for C. albicans)
Clinically notable for reduced susceptibility to fluconazole and other azoles

diseases: Candidemia and invasive candidiasis, particularly in hospitalized, elderly, or immunocompromised patients
Vulvovaginal candidiasis (a less common but recognized cause compared to C. albicans)
virulenceFactors: Biofilm formation on catheters and medical devices
Reduced/variable azole susceptibility contributing to persistent infection despite standard treatment
clinicalImportance.transmission: Usually endogenous, arising from the patient's own flora; healthcare-associated transmission via hands or contaminated devices is also recognized
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: One of the most common non-albicans Candida species causing candidemia, especially in older adults and those with prior azole exposure; a growing concern in antifungal stewardship due to reduced susceptibility to fluconazole
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Species identification and antifungal susceptibility testing are important once Candida is isolated from blood, since C. glabrata often requires higher-dose azoles or an alternative antifungal class (e.g., echinocandins)

examFacts.shape: Small budding yeast, no true hyphae
examFacts.importantDisease: Candidemia/invasive candidiasis with reduced azole susceptibility
examFacts.importantTest: Germ tube test (negative); species identification prompts antifungal susceptibility testing
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: A germ-tube-negative, non-hyphal Candida species notable for reduced fluconazole susceptibility, distinguishing its treatment from C. albicans
